title: Band-Saddle-Point Engineering in Mixed $A$-site $A$V$_3$Sb$_5$ Kagome Metals
authors: Maxim Wenzel, Alexander A. Tsirlin, Andrea N. Capa Salinas, Brenden R. Ortiz, Stephen D. Wilson, Ece Uykur, Martin Dressel
abstract: $A$V$_3$Sb$_5$ compounds ($A$ = K, Rb, Cs) offer an experimental platform for probing the physics of kagome metals near ideal Van Hove filling. Here, we use optical spectroscopy on $A$V$_3$Sb$_5$ with mixed $A$-site compositions to reveal the effect of the alkali metal on the low-energy electronic structure. Supported by density-functional-theory calculations, we identify a band-saddle-point inversion as a chemical consequence of Cs substitution, revealing that $A$-site composition controls the orbital character of Van Hove singularities, Fermi surface topology, and electron-phonon interactions while leaving the kagome layer intact.
summary: This study uses optical spectroscopy and DFT calculations on $	ext{AV}_3	ext{Sb}_5$ Kagome metals to map how changing the alkali metal site controls the electronic band structure and CDW physics. The key finding is that the A-site substitution drives a band-saddle-point inversion, and electronic correlations are highly sensitive to the resulting interlayer spacing. This work advances the understanding of correlation-driven phenomena in layered quantum magnets.
main_problem: The study investigates how varying the alkali metal composition (A-site substitution) in $	ext{AV}_3	ext{Sb}_5$ Kagome metals controls the low-energy electronic structure, particularly concerning the Charge-Density Wave (CDW) formation and orbital character.
main_result: The alkali site controls the orbital character of Van Hove singularities and Fermi surface topology, evidenced by a band-saddle-point inversion unique to Cs-containing compounds. Furthermore, electronic correlations are found to be sensitive to the interlayer distance, which is modulated by the A-site ion.
method: The research combines optical spectroscopy measurements with extensive Density-Functional-Theory (DFT) calculations to analyze band structures, electronic susceptibilities, and optical conductivity.
model_or_system: The system is the quasi-two-dimensional $	ext{AV}_3	ext{Sb}_5$ Kagome metal, where A is an alkali metal ($	ext{K}, 	ext{Rb}, 	ext{Cs}$). The physics is governed by the interplay between alkali substitution, electronic correlations, and CDW ordering.
key_observables: CDW gap ($2\Delta_{	ext{CDW}}$), interband optical conductivity features (especially around $200 	ext{ cm}^{-1}$), electronic correlation strength (via plasma frequency ratios), and the evolution of saddle-point electronic structure.
important_parameters: Alkali metal identity ($	ext{K}, 	ext{Rb}, 	ext{Cs}$), temperature (especially near $T_{	ext{CDW}}$), and the lattice interlayer distance.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on DFT calculations, which show discrepancies with experiment at low energies, necessitating assumptions like Fermi level renormalization to match observations.
figures_summary: Figures track the evolution of the CDW state and gap energy with A-site composition, compare experimental and DFT interband optical conductivity, and map the evolution of saddle-point electronic structure and Fermi surfaces.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the CDW state evolution, then delves into the electronic structure using DFT to pinpoint the role of the alkali ion via saddle-point inversion. It contrasts findings from different measurements (optical vs. susceptibility) to build a comprehensive picture of correlation effects.
why_interesting: The work provides a detailed case study of how chemical doping (A-site substitution) can tune fundamental electronic properties like orbital character and correlation strength in a highly correlated material, offering insights applicable to other layered quantum materials.
